extracted.intended_audience: health policymakers, funders, hospital administrators, haematologists and public-health practitioners interested in improving adult sickle-cell care
extracted.subtask_description: Recommendations and practical standards for building, funding and operating comprehensive adult sickle-cell services (clinical centres, hospital systems, surveillance and remote support) to close the care gap between paediatric and adult patients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund adult sickle-cell programmes at parity with paediatric ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Adult sickle-cell programmes should be funded like the paediatric ones are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: paediatric funding and the National Sickle Cell Anemia Control Act (1972) spurred multidisciplinary centres and large mortality reductions for children. Example: California used surveillance data to secure US$15 million from the state legislature to start adult sickle-cell centres. Policy implication: allocate dedicated, sustained public (or philanthropic) funding streams specifically for adult sickle-cell services rather than relying on ad hoc or smaller grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish comprehensive multidisciplinary adult sickle-cell centres
rubrics_metrics.description: Create centres that provide coordinated, multidisciplinary care for adults, analogous to successful paediatric models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essential team members: haematologists who specialize in sickle cell, emergency-department physicians familiar with the disease, social workers, psychologists, education specialists, nutritionists and specialists for organs commonly damaged by sickling (brain, kidneys). Evidence/example: there are only 49 adult centres versus 168 paediatric centres in the US; comparable diseases (cystic fibrosis, haemophilia) have >100 adult centres. Centres should enable specialist-directed care rather than fragmented primary-care management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not default complex sickle-cell management to general primary care
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid shifting adult sickle-cell care solely into primary care settings when the condition requires specialist knowledge and multidisciplinary resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: forcing adults into primary care because of lack of specialists. Reason: sickle-cell is multi-system and uncommon enough that primary-care providers cannot maintain expertise; they will prioritise more prevalent chronic diseases (e.g., diabetes). Instead, ensure specialist oversight or easy specialist consultation pathways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide structured transition services from paediatric to adult care
rubrics_metrics.description: Create transition programs so patients moving from paediatric to adult services do not lose access to coordinated care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Components: patient-care coordinators, social workers and reminder systems to maintain appointments; care navigation to prevent loss at transition age. Rationale: paediatric centres often have appointment reminders and coordinators that disappear at transition, leading to increased pain episodes and organ damage around age 18.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use surveillance data to plan services and leverage funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect statewide or regional surveillance data on sickle-cell prevalence and distribution to support planning and funding requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: CDC-funded statewide surveillance enabled California to make the funding case to legislators. Implementation: set up systematic data collection, analyse geographic distribution and use results to advocate for targeted centre placement and budgets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deploy telementoring to support remote and low-resource providers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use regular, structured telementoring (case-presentations and specialist panels) to enable generalists in remote/rural settings to provide informed sickle-cell care with virtual specialist support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model: weekly hour-long telementoring where remote providers present cases to a team including haematologists, psychiatrists/pain experts, social workers and community health workers. Benefit: flips telehealth by providing in-person care locally with virtual specialist guidance; scalable for systems without nearby centres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct patients without access to specialised centres to hospital complex-care teams
rubrics_metrics.description: When specialised sickle-cell centres are unavailable, hospitals should route patients to multidisciplinary complex-care teams already managing multi-system chronic conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of appropriate teams: those caring for patients with mental illness plus congestive heart failure or other complex co-morbidities. This provides a nearer-term substitute for a dedicated sickle-cell centre in smaller systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broaden adult access to hydroxyurea and ensure individualized, adequate dosing
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase hydroxyurea uptake among adults with sickle cell, and ensure dosing is tailored and sufficient to be effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: hydroxyurea reduces frequency and intensity of pain crises and is recommended for managing sickle cell; only ~30% of adults take it but ~80% might benefit. Practical notes: it requires individualized dosing, typical cost ~US$1,000/year; not effective for haemoglobin SC genotype and contraindicated in pregnancy. Implementation challenges: patient adherence (recommend trials of ~1 year), non-specialists often under-dose. Possible interventions: dosing support tools (e.g., mobile apps), specialist guidance, adherence support and monitoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement appropriate screening and acknowledge adult limitations (stroke/TCD example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt effective preventive screening where validated (eg, transcranial Doppler (TCD) for children) while recognising methods that do not work for adults and seeking alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TCD dramatically reduces paediatric stroke risk (from ~10% to 1–3%) by identifying high-risk children for transfusion and later hydroxyurea; however, TCD is not effective in adults. Policy implication: ensure children receive proven screens and invest in research or alternative adult risk-assessment methods rather than assuming paediatric tools transfer to adults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address structural racism and bias in care delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly confront systemic racism and anti-Black bias that produce disparities in resources and bedside treatment for people with sickle-cell disease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issues: populations with sickle cell are disproportionately Black or Latinx, face less wealth, insurance and research investment, and are more likely to have pain dismissed in emergency settings. Interventions: training to reduce bias, policy changes to ensure equitable resource allocation, and targeted programmes to correct historical under-investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve emergency-department triage and create dedicated ED pathways for sickle-cell crises
rubrics_metrics.description: Change triage protocols and ED structures so people with sickle-cell disease receive timely and appropriate acute pain management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: classifying all people with sickle-cell disease at the second-highest urgency level (recommended by the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality) improved appropriate triage from 30% to 85% in one system. Create observation units staffed by nurse practitioners/physician assistants with sickle-cell expertise; develop waiting-room treatment protocols; prioritise certain beds for sickle-cell patients to reduce time to first analgesia (example improvement from ~6 hours to ~2.5 hours).

rubrics_metrics.name: Create day hospitals, observation units and dedicated infusion clinics to manage crises outside the ED
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide alternatives to the emergency department for intravenous opioid administration and supportive care for acute pain crises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: faster, better and lower-cost care than ED; expands access to rapid opioid administration, anti-nausea and anti-itch treatments. Barriers: access for uninsured patients can be limited; dedicated infusion clinics and day hospitals require operational and funding investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use electronic medical-record nudges to prompt appropriate care
rubrics_metrics.description: Modify the electronic medical record (EMR) to flag sickle-cell patients and nudge providers toward evidence-based triage and treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete change: add a visible ribbon/flag indicating the disease and recommended urgency level; reported effect: improved appropriate triage rates. EMR nudges should be paired with clear protocols and clinician education to be effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure provider knowledge and protocols for opioid treatment of acute pain
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure providers, especially in acute-care settings, understand that opioids are the best treatment for acute sickle-cell crises and implement protocols to avoid dismissing patient-reported pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem: Black adults frequently have their pain discounted and are suspected of drug-seeking. Interventions: clinician education, standardised pain-assessment and analgesia protocols, rapid-treatment pathways, and systems to reduce security/expulsion responses when serious pathology (eg, acute chest syndrome) is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invest medical infrastructure in parallel with new drug development
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan and build the clinical and system infrastructure necessary to deliver and support new sickle-cell pharmaceuticals and therapies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: excitement and investment in drug development must be matched by clinics, specialist staffing, monitoring systems and equitable access pathways. Otherwise, new therapeutics will not achieve population-level benefit; coordination between research funding and care-infrastructure investment is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise equitable research, specialist training and resource allocation for diseases of marginalised groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct research funding, specialist training programs and centre-building efforts toward diseases that predominantly affect marginalised populations to correct historical underinvestment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context: diseases that affect more white people (eg, cystic fibrosis) have more centres and investment. Policy actions: shift funding priorities, incentivise specialist training in sickle-cell care, and ensure profitability assumptions do not determine research or service availability.
